case_name: Case 2 — Zero Tolerance, One Fee Increased
computation:
Zero-tolerance per-fee check:
  Origination Fee: CD $1,200 vs LE $1,000 → increase of $200 → VIOLATION
  Transfer Tax: CD $2,400 vs LE $2,500 → decrease of $100 → PASS (decreases are permitted)

Cure amount = $200 (the excess over the LE for the violating fee).

10% aggregate bucket: no fees — not applicable.
No-limit bucket: no fees — not applicable.
violations: Zero-tolerance bucket violated. Origination Fee increased by $200. Cure = $200, payable to the borrower.
clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(i): charges paid to the creditor are zero-tolerance; any increase is a violation regardless of whether other zero-tolerance fees decreased. The decrease in Transfer Tax does not offset the increase in Origination Fee because zero tolerance is checked per fee, not in aggregate.
weakest_point: Whether the cure must be credited to the borrower at or before consummation vs. within 30 days — the regulation's cure mechanism timing is not fully specified here.

case_name: Case 3 — 10% Aggregate, Mixed Directions, No Violation (aggregate-vs-aggregate vs. sum-of-increases distinction)
computation:
10% aggregate test — CORRECT method (aggregate CD vs aggregate LE + 10%):
  ΣLE = $500 + $400 + $300 + $200 = $1,400
  ΣCD = $600 + $300 + $350 + $220 = $1,470
  10% threshold = $1,400 × 0.10 = $140
  Tolerance limit = $1,400 + $140 = $1,540
  $1,470 ≤ $1,540 → PASS

INCORRECT method (sum of individual increases only — this is the common implementation error):
  Increases: Appraisal +$100, Title Search +$50, Recording +$20 = $170 total increases
  $170 > $140 threshold → would incorrectly FAIL

The distinction: the 10% test compares AGGREGATE CD to AGGREGATE LE + 10%. Decreases (Survey −$100) offset increases in the aggregate. The sum-of-increases method ignores offsets and overstates the violation.

Zero-tolerance bucket: no fees — not applicable.
No-limit bucket: no fees — not applicable.
violations: None. The 10% aggregate bucket passes under the correct aggregate-vs-aggregate test. A sum-of-increases implementation would incorrectly flag a violation.
clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii): the 10% cumulative tolerance is tested by comparing the aggregate of all charges in the category on the CD to the aggregate of all charges in the category on the LE. The regulation does not sum individual increases; it compares totals. Recording fees are explicitly included in this category. Services the borrower was permitted to shop for also fall here.
weakest_point: Whether appraisal, survey, and title search are correctly assigned to the 10% bucket depends on whether the creditor required these services AND permitted the borrower to shop — if the creditor required the appraisal but did NOT permit shopping, it would be zero tolerance instead. The bucket assignment assumes borrower was permitted to shop for all three.

computation:
10% aggregate test:
  ΣLE = $500 + $400 + $300 + $200 = $1,400
  ΣCD = $700 + $350 + $400 + $250 = $1,700
  10% threshold = $1,400 × 0.10 = $140
  Tolerance limit = $1,400 + $140 = $1,540
  $1,700 > $1,540 → VIOLATION
  Excess = $1,700 − $1,540 = $160

Note on mixed directions: Survey decreased by $50, which partially offsets the increases in the aggregate. The net aggregate increase is $300 ($1,700 − $1,400), not the sum of increases ($200 + $100 + $50 = $350). Even with the offset, the aggregate exceeds the tolerance limit.

Incorrect sum-of-increases method would yield: $350 > $140, excess = $210 — wrong cure amount.

Zero-tolerance bucket: no fees — not applicable.
No-limit bucket: no fees — not applicable.
violations: 10% aggregate bucket violated. Excess = $160. Cure = $160, payable to the borrower.
clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii): aggregate CD ($1,700) exceeds aggregate LE + 10% ($1,540) by $160. The creditor must cure the $160 excess. The aggregate comparison inherently accounts for mixed directions — decreases offset increases within the aggregate.
weakest_point: Whether the cure amount is $160 (correct per aggregate test) or allocated differently across individual fees — the regulation requires a lump-sum cure equal to the aggregate excess, not per-fee cures within the 10% bucket.

case_name: Case 5 — Mixed Buckets: Zero-Tolerance Violation + 10% Aggregate Pass + No-Limit Fees

fees.name: Homeowner's Insurance (prepaid, not a settlement service)
Optional Home Warranty (not required by creditor)

computation:
Zero-tolerance per-fee check:
  Origination Fee: CD $1,000 vs LE $1,000 → no increase → PASS
  Transfer Tax: CD $3,100 vs LE $3,000 → increase of $100 → VIOLATION
  Zero-tolerance cure = $100

10% aggregate test:
  ΣLE = $500 + $300 + $150 = $950
  ΣCD = $550 + $250 + $180 = $980
  10% threshold = $950 × 0.10 = $95
  Tolerance limit = $950 + $95 = $1,045
  $980 ≤ $1,045 → PASS
  (Mixed directions: Appraisal +$50, Survey −$50, Recording +$30; net aggregate increase = $30, well within $95 threshold)

No-limit bucket:
  Homeowner's Insurance: CD $1,500 vs LE $1,200 → increase of $300 → no tolerance test, no violation
  Optional Home Warranty: CD $600 vs LE $400 → increase of $200 → no tolerance test, no violation

Total cure = $100 (zero-tolerance violation only).
violations: Zero-tolerance bucket violated: Transfer Tax increased by $100. Cure = $100. The 10% aggregate bucket passes. The no-limit bucket has no tolerance test.
clause_basis: §1026.19(e)(3)(i): transfer taxes are zero-tolerance; the $100 increase is a violation. §1026.19(e)(3)(ii): recording fees and borrower-shoppable services are 10% aggregate; the aggregate CD ($980) does not exceed aggregate LE + 10% ($1,045). §1026.19(e)(3)(iii): homeowner's insurance and optional services not required by the creditor have no tolerance limit. Each bucket is tested independently — a violation in one bucket does not affect the others.
weakest_point: Whether homeowner's insurance is correctly in the no-limit bucket depends on whether the creditor required a specific insurance provider (which could move it to zero or 10% tolerance). The assignment assumes the borrower freely chose the insurer. Also, whether optional home warranty is truly 'not required' is a factual determination.
